missing_spec_content.spec_text: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never says that gas molecules move constantly and randomly. It only describes particles 'crashing into a container's walls' (intro) and moving faster when heated.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes. The pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container (or any surface).
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not say that the force from gas pressure acts at right angles to the wall or surface. It also does not state that pressure changes compress or expand a gas. keyPoints[0].content only says 'Each collision pushes on the wall with a tiny force'.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Work is the transfer of energy by a force. Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas. Students should be able to explain how, in a given situation eg a bicycle pump, doing work on an enclosed gas leads to an increase in the temperature of the gas.
missing_spec_content.why: This whole section (HT only) is missing. The intro mentions 'pump up a bike tyre' but never explains that doing work on the gas transfers energy, raises its internal energy and raises its temperature. Internal energy is not mentioned anywhere.

above_gcse.text: When the temperature can change too, use the combined gas law. It is p₁V₁ / T₁ = p₂V₂ / T₂, where T is in Kelvin.
above_gcse.why: The specification only requires pV = constant at constant temperature. The combined gas law is not in these sections.

above_gcse.text: Worked example: a gas is at 100 kPa, 2 m³ and 300 K. It is heated to 600 K at constant volume. New pressure: p₂ = p₁ × T₂ / T₁ = 100 × 600/300 = 200 kPa.
above_gcse.why: The spec asks students to 'explain qualitatively the relation between the temperature of a gas and its pressure at constant volume'. Calculations using p/T are not required.
This named law, with p/T = constant, is not in the specification. The spec only requires a qualitative relation.

above_gcse.text: Charles's Law | Pressure (p) | V and T directly proportional | V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂
above_gcse.why: The volume–temperature relationship at constant pressure is not in the specification sections at all.

above_gcse.text: Combined Gas Law | Mass of gas | Links p, V and T | p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂
above_gcse.why: The combined gas law is not required by the specification.

above_gcse.text: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero: 0 K = −273 °C ... To convert: T (K) = θ (°C) + 273 ... You must always use Kelvin in gas law calculations
above_gcse.why: Absolute zero, the Kelvin scale and conversion between scales do not appear in these specification sections. Kelvin is only needed for the quantitative temperature laws, which are themselves beyond the spec.

above_gcse.text: A gas in a container with a fixed volume is at 200 kPa and 300 K. It is heated to 450 K. What is the new pressure?
above_gcse.why: This tests a calculation of pressure from temperature. The spec only requires a qualitative explanation.
Kelvin conversion is not required by these specification sections.

above_gcse.text: If T changes, use pV/T = constant.
above_gcse.why: This tells students to use an equation the specification does not include.

factual_errors.text: At absolute zero, particles have the least kinetic energy possible. In theory, they stop moving completely.
factual_errors.correction: At absolute zero, particles have the minimum possible energy, but quantum theory says they do not stop moving completely (zero-point energy). It is safer to say 'particles have the minimum possible kinetic energy'.

factual_errors.text: At absolute zero, particles have the least kinetic energy. In theory, they stop moving
factual_errors.correction: Same issue: at absolute zero, particle energy is at its minimum, not zero motion.

factual_errors.text: At 0 K the pressure would be zero. Particles would have no kinetic energy and make no collisions.
factual_errors.correction: Zero pressure at 0 K is an extrapolation for an ideal gas. Real gases liquefy or solidify long before 0 K. Particles do not have exactly zero kinetic energy at 0 K.

wrong_terms.text: Gas pressure is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container
wrong_terms.spec_term: molecules (the spec says 'The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion' and 'the motion of the molecules in a gas')

wrong_terms.text: Boyle's Law — pressure and volume at constant temperature
wrong_terms.spec_term: The spec does not name the law. It says 'For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature: pressure × volume = constant, p V = constant'.

wrong_terms.text: Units: pressure in Pa (pascals) or kPa. Volume in m³ or cm³.
wrong_terms.spec_term: pressure, p, in pascals, Pa; volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3
